title: Short Stuff: The Amazing Tale of Juliane Koepcke
summary: Short Stuff episode on Juliane Koepcke, a German-born teenager who survived the 1971 LANSA Flight 508 crash in Peru after the plane was struck by lightning and broke up mid-air. Josh and Chuck cover her upbringing in the Peruvian jungle with her zoologist father and ornithologist mother at the Panguana research station, the crash over the Amazon on Christmas Eve 1971 with 92 aboard (91 killed, including her mother), her eleven days alone in the jungle following a river to a forest workers' shack, the wreckage she found on day four, the Werner Herzog documentary Wings of Hope, and her later work preserving Panguana, earning a biology doctorate focused on bats, and taking over the preserve after her father's death in 2000.

segments.title: Opening and why the story is trending
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and says Juliane Koepcke's story has resurfaced widely over the past year. Chuck recommends the Werner Herzog documentary Wings of Hope.

segments.title: Childhood in the Peruvian jungle
segments.summary: Koepcke grew up in the Peruvian jungle, where her parents, a zoologist father and an ornithologist mother, founded the Panguana research station. She learned the local animals and how to survive there before attending private school in Lima.

segments.title: Lightning strike and mid-air breakup
segments.summary: On Christmas Eve 1971, Koepcke, age 17, was flying with her mother toward her father when the plane hit severe turbulence, was struck by lightning, and broke apart at about 10,000 feet. She was still strapped into her seat as it fell, and she was the only one of 92 people aboard to survive.

segments.title: Ad-free crash aftermath and search for her mother
segments.summary: Josh describes the crash as the worst lightning strike disaster in aviation history, with 91 of 92 dying including her mother. Koepcke spent the first days looking for her mother and anyone else alive.

segments.title: Wreckage discovery in the jungle
segments.summary: On about the fourth day, Koepcke found wreckage with three bodies still strapped to their seats, buried headfirst. She checked the feet for painted toenails to rule out that one was her mother. Josh and Chuck discuss the grim scene.

segments.title: Eleven days alone following the river
segments.summary: Koepcke recalled her father's advice to find water and follow it to people. She survived on river water and little food during the wet season, following a creek that grew into a river for eleven days until she found a boat and a shack of forest workers.

segments.title: Rescue and infected wounds
segments.summary: The forest workers gave Koepcke fruit and treated her wounds. Josh cites a New York Times article by Franz Litz describing maggots in her wounds, and notes how severe her nearsightedness was without her glasses.

segments.title: Reunion, Herzog film and Panguana preservation
segments.summary: Koepcke was flown to safety and reunited with her father. She avoided the media except for Werner Herzog, who was scouting for a project and had been expected on the flight; he made Wings of Hope, in which she returned to the wreckage site. Afterward she used her profile to raise funds to preserve Panguana, which grew from about 445 acres to over 4,000.

segments.title: Later career with bats and running Panguana
segments.summary: Koepcke earned a doctorate in biology focused on bats and worked with her father. After his death in 2000 she took over the Panguana Biosphere Preserve and research station, which she still runs and considers her sanctuary.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up, with a brief joke about the story, and the episode closes with the standard show and iHeartRadio credit.
